question: Open question: can pseudolabeler-aware contrastive pretraining improve weak-to-strong?
asked_by: Lang et al., Theoretical Analysis of Weak-to-Strong Generalization
remaining_question: Does making the contrastive pretraining objective aware of the pseudolabeler ỹ (e.g. defining or weighting positive pairs with the weak labels) lower the strong student's error on the true labels compared with pseudolabeler-agnostic contrastive pretraining under the same weak labels, and if so, does the gain come with greater measured expansion between correctly and incorrectly pseudolabeled sets?

blockers.name: A measurement
blockers.next: Pretrain the strong student with a pseudolabeler-aware and with a pseudolabeler-agnostic contrastive objective under the same weak labels, compare its error on the true labels, and measure expansion between correctly and incorrectly pseudolabeled sets.

findings.claim: ConG uses contrastive decoding between the pre- and post-alignment weak models to generate higher-quality training samples for the strong model, motivated by a structural equivalence between implicit rewards and contrastive decoding; the authors report consistent improvements across model families. 'Contrastive' here refers to decoding of the weak supervisor's outputs, not to the strong student's (pre)training objective.
findings.setting: LLM weak-to-strong alignment with samples generated by aligned weak models; empirical; no representation pretraining.
findings.bears_on: Near miss for the question's 'contrastive' ingredient: it changes how weak supervision is generated, not how the student is pretrained.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2412.03881v2: Weak-to-Strong Generalization Through the Data-Centric Lens
findings.claim: Building on Lang et al.'s framework, the authors identify overlap points and give an algorithm that estimates which of several data sources has the largest overlap density, recommending investment in data from sources likely to produce overlaps rather than in algorithms.
findings.setting: Theory building on Lang et al.'s framework plus an algorithm that estimates which of several data sources has the largest overlap density; intervention on data acquisition, not on pretraining.
findings.bears_on: An alternative, data-side way to exploit the expansion framework the question appeals to; does not test contrastive pretraining.

passages.text:
Equipped with this intuition, we characterize the notion of overlap and provide theoretical results
building on a recent theoretical framework for generalization (Lang et al., 2024). In practice, however,
overlap points are latent, and it can be difficult to distinguish between points with just an easy pattern
and those with overlaps. To address this challenge, we introduce an approach for identifying points
with overlaps and build on it to obtain an algorithm that can, when presented with multiple sources of
data, estimate which one contains the largest overlap density. This suggests a future course of action
for practitioners focused on maximizing weak-to-strong generalization: rather than focusing on
algorithms, invest in the data—and specifically into obtaining data from sources that are likely to
produce the most overlaps.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2605.05710v1: On the Blessing of Pre-training in Weak-to-Strong Generalization
findings.claim: In a high-dimensional single-index model with spiked Gaussian data, modeling pretraining as a spectral initialization step (PCA), the authors prove W2S is achievable when pretraining gives a geometric warm start into an effective region, with a generalization bound showing improvement then saturation set by the weak supervisor's bias; they note the PCA proxy may not capture nonlinear feature learning in large models.
findings.setting: Theory: single-index model, spiked Gaussian data, pretraining modelled as an unsupervised spectral initialization step (PCA) that does not see the pseudolabeler; a stylised theoretical model, not contrastive or pseudolabeler-aware pretraining.
findings.bears_on: Links a spectral (pseudolabeler-agnostic) pretraining step to W2S success; does not make pretraining aware of the weak labels.

The paradigm of Weak-to-Strong Generalization (W2SG) suggests that a pretrained strong model can surpass its weak supervisor, yet the decisive role of
pre-training remains theoretically and empirically under-explored. In this work,
we identify pre-training as the essential prerequisite for the emergence of W2SG.
Theoretically, we formalize the W2SG problem within a high-dimensional singleindex model framework using spiked Gaussian data, modeling pre-training as a
spectral initialization step. Building upon prior impossibility results regarding the
failure of learning under random initialization, we prove that W2SG is achievable
when pre-training provides a geometric warm start that places the model within an
“effective region” characterized by a perturbed strong-convexity geometry. Within
